vignette:
Rangi Parata is a fifty-one-year-old Māori man who works as a welder at a fabrication yard on the outskirts of Tacoma, Washington. He has been married for twenty-two years, and until recently his life had a steady, physical rhythm - early starts, long shifts, the familiar smell of hot metal and flux, evenings at home with his wife. That rhythm was broken fourteen months ago on a Friday night when a drunk driver ran a red light and struck the driver's side of Rangi's truck at highway speed. The impact crumpled the door into his left hip and shoulder, pinned him at an angle against the centre console, and left him conscious and trapped for nearly forty minutes while emergency crews worked to free him. He could smell the alcohol on the other driver's breath from several feet away through the shattered window. He could hear metal groaning, other cars slowing and stopping, someone shouting his name. He was certain, in those forty minutes, that he was going to die in that position.

He did not die, but the memory of the collision has not behaved like a memory. In the months following the crash, Rangi found that when the recollection returned - uninvited, without warning - it did not arrive as a narrative he could observe from a distance. Instead, it arrived as a full sensory event: the smell of alcohol, the sound of bending steel, the weight of the door against his hip, the specific angle at which his body had been forced. He would feel his shoulder compress and his left side brace, as though the impact were happening again in real time. He would feel pain - genuine, localised pain - in the hip and shoulder that had been injured, even when he was sitting quietly at his kitchen table or lying in bed. The reliving was not a flashback in the way he had imagined the word; it was, as he described it to his wife, "being back inside it, completely, all at once."

What has followed from the nature of that memory is that the world around Rangi has become densely populated with ways back in. Because the reliving carries the full sensory texture of the original event - the smell, the sounds, the bodily posture - any fragment of that texture is enough to pull the memory forward. The smell of alcohol, which he now encounters whenever colleagues crack open beers after a Friday shift, has become almost unbearable; he has begun leaving the yard early on Fridays, telling his foreman he has errands, because he has learned that staying means the evening will be lost to pain and fear. At the fabrication yard itself, the sounds of cars in the adjacent lot - engines idling, doors slamming, the particular pitch of a vehicle braking hard on gravel - can trigger the same process mid-shift, so that Rangi finds himself gripping his welding torch and waiting for the physical sensation of impact that his body insists is coming. Images of damaged vehicles, which he cannot entirely avoid given that accident scenes appear on the news and on roadside hoardings, carry the same charge; his wife has noticed that he now leaves the room when traffic reports come on television.

The consequence has been a quiet but significant narrowing of his life. He drives a different route to work to avoid the intersection where the crash occurred. He has declined two social invitations that involved evening driving. His wife has described feeling that she is "managing around him" without fully understanding what she is managing. Rangi himself has not been able to explain it to her in terms that satisfy either of them, partly because he does not understand why a smell or a sound should produce physical pain in a healed shoulder - and that confusion has begun to feel like its own kind of threat, the possibility that something is permanently wrong with him that no one has named.

What finally brought him to seek help was a shift three weeks ago when the sound of a car braking sharply outside the yard triggered a reliving episode so complete - pain, posture, smell, the certainty of dying - that a colleague thought he was having a medical emergency. Rangi is hoping, cautiously, to understand what is happening to his body. What he is most afraid of is that the answer will confirm what he already suspects: that he will never be free of it.
